Runtime.0002.description:
Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.
Runtime.0002.title: Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience

links.title: Upgrade to latest .NET with Upgrade Assistant

Scale.0001.description:
Static content detected.

Your current approach of serving static content directly might lead to increased costs, performance issues, maintenance challenges (requiring application redeployment for content changes), and security risks.

Consider moving static content to Azure Blob Storage and adding Azure CDN.
Scale.0001.title: Static content detected

Local.0007.description:
Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Local.0007.title: Local OS environment access detected

links.title: App Service sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps

Logging.0103.description: Log4Net logging framework detected. Log4Net is an older logging framework with limited cloud-native capabilities. Consider migrating to OpenTelemetry for modern observability, better performance, and seamless Azure Monitor integration.
Logging.0103.title: Log4Net logging framework detected

Local.0004.description:
Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.
Local.0004.title: Logging to local or network paths detected

Connection.0001.description:
Connection string detected. It may not be available when your app is migrated to Azure.

Review and ensure it works from Azure. If you are connecting to a database, you might need to migrate the database to Azure. There are multiple ways to do it:
    1. Migrate to Azure SQL Database for additional benefits (see the link below).
    2. Consider Azure SQL Managed Instance if you need features that are not available in Azure SQL Database and you don’t want to use a VM.
    3. Migrate your database servers directly to SQL Server on Azure VMs.

To assess database migration effort, you can use Azure Migrate tool, see the link below.
Connection.0001.title: Connection string is detected

links.title: Migrate SQL Server database to Azure

Database.0003.description:
System.Data.SqlClient dependency is detected.

While System.Data.SqlClient will work in Azure, the newer Microsoft.Data.SqlClient package is the primary .NET SQL client moving forward and receiving the latest features. For example, Microsoft.Data.SqlClient easily allows use of Azure Managed Identity from a connection string.
Database.0003.title: System.Data.SqlClient dependency detected

Identity.0002.description:
Your app is using windows authentication which is not supported on Azure App Service, Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service.

Azure App Service provides built-in authentication and authorization capabilities, so you can sign in users and access data by writing minimal or no code in your web app.

Follow the link below for more information."
Identity.0002.title: Windows authentication detected

Scale.0002.description:
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.
Scale.0002.title: Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected

links.title: ASP.NET Session State Provider for Azure Cache for Redis
Use Azure Cosmos DB as an ASP.NET session state and caching provider
Azure Cosmos DB: autoscale, session state, monitoring, and more

Security.0002.description:
Connection strings without configuration builders detected.  

 Keeping connection strings directly in the app is not the best practice and might introduce security risks, increased maintenance, scalability challenges or compliance standards (such as PCI DSS, GDPR, etc.). 

 Instead, it is recommended to use configuration builders to get secrets from secure sources in Azure environment.
Security.0002.title: Connection strings without configuration builders detected

Local.0003.description:
Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
    1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
    2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
    3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.
Local.0003.title: Local or network IO operations detected

Configuration.0003.description: Local application configuration detected. Azure App Configuration can be used as a centralized, cloud-based service for application settings that are currently stored in local configuration files. Moving this configuration to Azure App Configuration can help you externalize settings from code and deployment artifacts, centralize management across environments, and enable dynamic refresh and controlled access to configuration data.
Configuration.0003.title: Local application configuration detected

links.title: Configuration management with Azure App Configuration

security.Name: Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions in Newtonsoft.Json
security.Description:
[CVE-2024-21907](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5crp-9r3c-p9vr): Newtonsoft.Json versions before 13.0.1 can consume excessive CPU and memory or trigger a StackOverflowException when processing highly nested JSON, resulting in denial of service.

Severity: HIGH

Affected dependencies:
  - Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1 (declared at src/eShopLegacyMVC/packages.config:29 and referenced in src/eShopLegacyMVC/eShopLegacyMVC.csproj:102)

Recommended fix:
  - Upgrade Newtonsoft.Json to 13.0.1 or later.
security.Explanation:
[CVE-2024-21907](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5crp-9r3c-p9vr): Newtonsoft.Json versions before 13.0.1 can consume excessive CPU and memory or trigger a StackOverflowException when processing highly nested JSON, resulting in denial of service.

Severity: HIGH

Affected dependencies:
  - Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.1 (declared at src/eShopLegacyMVC/packages.config:29 and referenced in src/eShopLegacyMVC/eShopLegacyMVC.csproj:102)

Recommended fix:
  - Upgrade Newtonsoft.Json to 13.0.1 or later.

security.Name: Incorrect Conversion between Numeric Types
security.Description: When converting from one data type to another, such as long to integer, data can be omitted or translated in a way that produces unexpected values. If the resulting values are used in a sensitive context, then dangerous behaviors may occur.
security.Explanation: CatalogItemHiLoGenerator.GetNextSequenceValue reads a database sequence as Int64 and casts the value to int without a range check (CatalogItemHiLoGenerator.cs:22-23). CatalogDBInitializer.GetSequenceIdFromSelectedDBSequence performs the same narrowing conversion (CatalogDBInitializer.cs:326-329). Values outside the Int32 range can wrap/truncate and produce incorrect identifiers.

security.Name: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value
security.Description: The product allocates memory based on an untrusted, large size value, but it does not ensure that the size is within expected limits, allowing arbitrary amounts of memory to be allocated.
security.Explanation: CatalogController.Index accepts pageSize directly from the request and applies no upper bound before passing it to the service (CatalogController.cs:22-25). CatalogService uses that value in Take(pageSize) and materializes the rows with ToList (CatalogService.cs:23-31), permitting a caller to request and allocate an unbounded page of catalog records.

security.Name: Use of Singleton Pattern Without Synchronization in a Multithreaded Context
security.Description: The product uses the singleton pattern when creating a resource within a multithreaded environment.
security.Explanation: When UseMockData is enabled, ApplicationModule registers CatalogServiceMock as a SingleInstance. The singleton owns a mutable List<CatalogItem> that is read and modified by service methods without synchronization, so concurrent MVC/Web API requests can race.

security.Name: Unsynchronized Access to Shared Data in a Multithreaded Context
security.Description: The product does not properly synchronize shared data, such as static variables across threads, which can lead to undefined behavior and unpredictable data changes.
security.Explanation: With UseMockData enabled, one CatalogServiceMock instance and its mutable catalogItems list are shared across requests. CreateCatalogItem, UpdateCatalogItem, and RemoveCatalogItem mutate the list while query methods enumerate/read it, and these operations have no lock or concurrent collection.

security.Name: Improper Synchronization
security.Description: The product utilizes multiple threads or processes to allow temporary access to a shared resource that can only be exclusive to one process at a time, but it does not properly synchronize these actions, which might cause simultaneous accesses of this resource by multiple threads or processes.
security.Explanation: The mock service is registered as a singleton when enabled, making its catalog list a shared resource. Concurrent request handlers perform reads and writes to that list without mutual exclusion, allowing conflicting updates and enumeration during mutation.

security.Name: Missing Synchronization
security.Description: The product utilizes a shared resource in a concurrent manner but does not attempt to synchronize access to the resource.
security.Explanation: The singleton CatalogServiceMock exposes its shared mutable catalogItems list to concurrent requests, but its list reads and mutations are not protected by synchronization.

security.Name: Incorrect Synchronization
security.Description: The product utilizes a shared resource in a concurrent manner, but it does not correctly synchronize access to the shared resource.
security.Explanation: In mock mode the singleton CatalogServiceMock shares a mutable list across requests without protecting read or write operations. The separate lock in CatalogItemHiLoGenerator does not cover this list.

security.Name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
security.Description: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that is intended to identify a file or directory that is located underneath a restricted parent directory, but the product does not properly neutralize special elements within the pathname that can cause the pathname to resolve to a location that is outside of the restricted directory.
security.Explanation: PicController.Index combines the Pics web root with item.PictureFileName and reads the resulting path (PicController.cs:38-44) without validating that it remains beneath the root. CatalogController.Create and Edit bind PictureFileName from submitted model data (CatalogController.cs:62, 100), allowing a stored value containing traversal elements or a rooted path to reach the file read.

security.Name: Relative Path Traversal
security.Description: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that should be within a restricted directory, but it does not properly neutralize sequences such as .. that can resolve to a location that is outside of that directory.
security.Explanation: PicController.Index passes item.PictureFileName from the catalog to Path.Combine(webRoot, ...) and then reads the returned file path (PicController.cs:39, 44). The filename is accepted from submitted CatalogItem data by CatalogController.Create (CatalogController.cs:62); relative path segments such as .. are not neutralized or checked against the Pics directory.

security.Name: Absolute Path Traversal
security.Description: The product uses external input to construct a pathname that should be within a restricted directory, but it does not properly neutralize absolute path sequences such as /abs/path that can resolve to a location that is outside of that directory.
security.Explanation: PicController.Index passes the catalog item's PictureFileName directly as the second Path.Combine argument (PicController.cs:39). Because Create binds PictureFileName from request data (CatalogController.cs:62), a rooted filename can select a path outside the Pics directory; no containment check is performed before File.ReadAllBytes.

security.Name: Improper Control of Resource Identifiers ('Resource Injection')
security.Description: The product receives input from an upstream component, but it does not restrict or incorrectly restricts the input before it is used as an identifier for a resource that may be outside the intended sphere of control.
security.Explanation: CatalogController.Create binds the request-supplied PictureFileName into a catalog item (CatalogController.cs:62). PicController.Index uses that value to identify and read a file after combining it with the Pics directory without restricting the resulting resource to that directory (PicController.cs:39-44).

security.Name: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
security.Description: The product deserializes untrusted data without sufficiently ensuring that the resulting data will be valid.
security.Explanation: Serializing.DeserializeBinary accepts a caller-provided Stream and passes it directly to BinaryFormatter.Deserialize without a binder or validation of the serialized types (Serializing.cs:16-20). No current call site for DeserializeBinary was found, so reachability from an external request was not established; the unsafe deserialization API is nevertheless present in the solution.
